title: Lesson 4: Receiving Corrections Without Hostility
summary: Correction is a normal part of maintaining standards. Listen, examine the facts, and respond without anger, insults or retaliation.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Humility, respectful responses, accountability, receiving feedback and professional growth

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a therapist at Zura Spa has just completed a massage session.
A supervisor notices that the treatment room has not been properly arranged for the next client.
The supervisor says: "Please ensure that the used towels are removed, the bed is properly prepared and the room is checked before the next appointment."
The therapist becomes angry. She replies: "Why are you always disturbing me? Am I the only person working here?" She walks away and refuses to continue the conversation.
The supervisor's correction was intended to address a work-related issue, but the employee's hostile reaction has created another problem.

Now consider a different response. The therapist listens and says: "Understood. I missed the towel replacement. I'll correct it now and ensure I check the room before the next appointment." The problem is addressed without unnecessary conflict.
Both employees received a correction. One turned it into a confrontation; the other used it as an opportunity to improve.
At Zura Spa, employees should understand that correction is a normal part of maintaining service standards.
Being corrected does not mean an employee is worthless, incompetent or personally disliked. It means that a particular action, decision or result requires attention.
However, corrections must also be communicated respectfully. Employees are expected to respond professionally, not to tolerate insults, threats or humiliation.

sections.title: 2. What does receiving correction without hostility mean?
paragraphs: Receiving correction without hostility means listening to feedback, examining the concern and responding respectfully without unnecessary aggression, insults, threats or retaliation.
It does not mean agreeing with every statement.
It does not mean accepting blame for something you did not do.
It does not mean remaining silent when a correction is inaccurate or unfair.
An employee can disagree with a correction and still remain professional.

items.label: Evaluating
items.body: Considering whether the correction is accurate and what needs improvement.

items.label: Responding
items.body: Communicating respectfully and taking appropriate action.

sections.title: 3. Understanding the difference between correction and hostility
paragraphs: Correction is intended to identify an issue and help improve behaviour, performance or outcomes.
Hostility involves aggressive, disrespectful or antagonistic behaviour directed at another person.
Correction should address the work, not attack the employee's dignity.
Similarly, receiving correction should not become an excuse to insult the person giving it.
table: "Please replace the towels before the next appointment."
"You are so careless. Can't you do anything properly?"
"The client requested lighter pressure. Please adjust accordingly."
"You clearly don't know how to do your job."
"This task needs to be completed before 4 p.m."
"If you had any sense, you would have finished this already."

sections.title: 1. It supports personal improvement
paragraphs: Employees can identify mistakes and develop better work habits.

sections.title: 2. It strengthens teamwork
paragraphs: Colleagues can raise genuine concerns without every conversation becoming an argument.

sections.title: 3. It protects service quality
paragraphs: Correcting errors promptly helps maintain appropriate standards for clients.

sections.title: 4. It demonstrates emotional maturity
paragraphs: Employees show that they can handle uncomfortable feedback without unnecessary aggression.

sections.title: 5. It improves communication
paragraphs: Feedback becomes a conversation about solutions rather than a personal confrontation.

sections.title: 6. It builds professional credibility
paragraphs: Employees who respond responsibly to feedback demonstrate reliability and willingness to learn.

sections.title: A. Raising one's voice
paragraphs: Speaking loudly or aggressively can turn a simple correction into a confrontation.

sections.title: B. Insulting the person giving correction
paragraphs: Statements such as "You're stupid" or "You don't know anything" are inappropriate workplace responses.

sections.title: C. Walking away angrily
paragraphs: Leaving a conversation without explanation may prevent the concern from being resolved.
If an employee genuinely needs a moment to regain composure, she can request a brief pause respectfully.

sections.title: D. Blaming others immediately
paragraphs: Mentioning another employee's mistakes does not automatically address your own responsibility.

sections.title: E. Using sarcasm
paragraphs: Statements such as "Since you know everything, why don't you do it yourself?" create unnecessary hostility.

sections.title: F. Refusing to cooperate
paragraphs: An employee may deliberately ignore an instruction because she is upset about receiving correction.

sections.title: G. Retaliating afterward
paragraphs: Gossiping, excluding colleagues, withholding cooperation or attempting to embarrass the person who gave feedback can damage teamwork.
Correction should lead to understanding and improvement, not retaliation.

sections.title: 6. Why some employees react with hostility
paragraphs: Hostile reactions may arise from several emotional triggers.
Understanding these triggers does not excuse hostile behaviour.
It helps employees recognise why they may be reacting strongly and choose a more appropriate response.

sections.title: 7. Seven principles for receiving correction without hostility
Principle 1: Listen before responding
paragraphs: Allow the person to explain the concern.
Avoid interrupting simply because the feedback is uncomfortable.

sections.title: Principle 2: Separate the correction from your identity
paragraphs: A mistake does not define your entire ability or worth.
For example, forgetting to replenish massage oil does not automatically mean you are an incompetent therapist.

sections.title: Principle 3: Manage your tone and body language
paragraphs: Avoid shouting, mocking, eye-rolling or aggressive gestures.

sections.title: Principle 4: Ask questions when necessary
paragraphs: If the feedback is unclear, request specific details.
Example: "Could you explain which part of the preparation needs improvement?"

sections.title: Principle 5: Acknowledge genuine mistakes
paragraphs: If you made an error, accept responsibility.
Example: "You're right. I forgot to replace the towels. I'll correct it now."

sections.title: Principle 6: Explain your perspective respectfully
paragraphs: If the correction is inaccurate, clarify the facts without insulting the person.
Example: "I understand the concern, but I completed the preparation before the room was used again. Could we review what happened?"

sections.title: Principle 7: Follow through on the correction
paragraphs: Receiving feedback professionally includes taking the appropriate action afterward.
A polite acknowledgment without improvement may not resolve the problem.

sections.title: 8. The difference between humility and humiliation
paragraphs: Humility means recognising that you can learn, improve and sometimes be wrong.
Humiliation means being made to feel degraded, embarrassed or inferior.
These are not the same.
Employees should practise humility, while supervisors and colleagues should avoid humiliating others.
A respectful workplace requires both responsibilities.

sections.title: Humility looks like
list: Listening to feedback.
Acknowledging mistakes.
Asking questions.
Accepting guidance.
Seeking improvement.
Treating others respectfully.

sections.title: Humiliation may involve
list: Public insults.
Mockery.
Threats.
Personal attacks.
Deliberate embarrassment.
Degrading language.

sections.title: 9. How to respond when correction is given in front of others
paragraphs: Public correction can be embarrassing.
Sometimes an immediate instruction is necessary, particularly when client safety or service quality is affected.
However, detailed performance feedback is often better handled privately when practical.
If the correction involves public humiliation or repeated inappropriate treatment, the employee may raise the concern through an appropriate reporting channel.

sections.title: Example — a public room-cleaning instruction
paragraphs: A supervisor says in front of colleagues: "Please ensure the treatment room is properly cleaned before the next appointment."
The employee may respond: "Understood. I'll address it now."
If she feels the issue requires further discussion, she can add: "Could we discuss the details privately afterward?"
This response addresses the immediate operational concern while protecting the opportunity for a respectful conversation.

sections.title: 10. Receiving correction from colleagues
paragraphs: Employees should not assume that only supervisors can identify mistakes.
Colleagues may notice issues affecting shared responsibilities.
The relevant issue is the client's preference, not whether the receptionist holds a supervisory position.
However, colleagues should also communicate corrections respectfully and avoid acting beyond their responsibilities.

sections.title: Example — a client's pressure preference
paragraphs: A receptionist informs a therapist: "The client has requested lighter pressure. Please make sure the preference is followed."
Hostile response: "Don't tell me how to do my job!"
Professional response: "Thank you for letting me know. I'll confirm the client's preference and adjust appropriately."

sections.title: 11. Receiving correction from clients
paragraphs: Clients may provide feedback about service quality, comfort or preferences.
Employees should not interpret every complaint as a personal attack.
Client feedback should be taken seriously, particularly when it relates to comfort, consent or safety.
Employees should also maintain appropriate professional boundaries and seek assistance when a client behaves abusively or inappropriately.

sections.title: Example — massage pressure too firm
paragraphs: A client says: "The massage pressure is too firm."
Hostile response: "That's how the massage is supposed to be."
Professional response: "Thank you for letting me know. I'll reduce the pressure. Please tell me if you would like it adjusted further."

sections.title: 12. What to do when a correction is inaccurate
paragraphs: Employees may sometimes receive correction based on incomplete or incorrect information.
Receiving correction without hostility does not mean accepting false blame.
Professional disagreement is not hostility.

sections.title: Example — Room 3 already prepared
paragraphs: A supervisor says: "You failed to prepare Room 3." The employee knows she completed the preparation earlier.
Hostile response: "You don't know what you're talking about!"
Professional response: "I understand the concern. I completed the room preparation at 2 p.m., but the room was used afterward. Could we check the timeline before deciding what happened?"

sections.title: Appropriate steps
list: Listen to the concern.
Identify the disputed information.
Explain the facts calmly.
Provide relevant evidence if available.
Request clarification or a fair review.
Escalate appropriately if necessary.

sections.title: 13. The CALM method for receiving correction

items.label: C — Control your immediate reaction
items.body: Avoid responding impulsively with anger or aggression.

items.label: A — Assess the feedback
items.body: Listen carefully and identify the actual concern.

items.label: L — Learn and clarify
items.body: Ask questions, examine the facts and identify what needs improvement.

items.label: M — Make the necessary adjustment
items.body: Correct genuine mistakes and follow through on agreed actions.

sections.title: CALM example
paragraphs: A supervisor notices that an appointment was recorded incorrectly.
The receptionist feels embarrassed but applies CALM.
She listens, checks the booking details, acknowledges the error and corrects the record.
She then confirms the updated information with the relevant staff.
The issue is resolved without unnecessary conflict.

sections.title: 14. Giving corrections respectfully: The responsibility of supervisors and colleagues
paragraphs: Receiving correction professionally is important, but the person giving correction also has responsibilities.
A culture of respectful correction makes it easier for employees to acknowledge mistakes and improve.

sections.title: Good correction should be
list: Specific: Explain what needs improvement.
Factual: Avoid unsupported accusations.
Respectful: Do not insult or humiliate.
Timely: Address concerns while they can still be corrected.
Fair: Consider relevant circumstances.
Constructive: Explain the expected improvement.
Open to clarification: Allow the employee to respond.

sections.title: Example — unhelpful versus constructive correction
paragraphs: Unhelpful correction: "You're always careless. I don't know why you can't do anything right."

Constructive correction: "The room was missing clean towels before the appointment. Please ensure the room checklist is completed before the next client. Is there any difficulty preventing you from doing this?"

sections.title: Case study A: The therapist who shouted
paragraphs: A supervisor points out that a treatment room was not fully prepared.
The therapist raises her voice and accuses the supervisor of unfair treatment.
Expected lesson: Employees should respond to correction without aggression while retaining the right to clarify concerns.
list: What emotional trigger may have influenced the therapist?
Which part of her response was hostile?
How could she respond professionally?
What should the supervisor do to maintain a respectful conversation?
What action would resolve the original problem?

sections.title: Case study B: The receptionist who made an error
paragraphs: A receptionist enters an incorrect appointment time.
When the error is identified, she becomes embarrassed and blames another employee.
Expected lesson: Acknowledging genuine mistakes supports trust and improvement.
list: What mistake occurred?
Why might the receptionist feel defensive?
How did blame-shifting affect accountability?
What would be a better response?
How could the team prevent similar errors?

sections.title: Case study C: The colleague's feedback
paragraphs: A therapist notices that another therapist has not replenished the room supplies.
She raises the concern politely. The other therapist becomes offended and refuses to cooperate with her afterward.
Expected lesson: Employees should not retaliate against colleagues for raising legitimate work-related concerns.
list: Was the feedback necessarily a personal attack?
What made the response hostile?
How could the employee handle the feedback differently?
What should happen if the disagreement continues?

sections.title: Case study D: The unfair correction
paragraphs: An employee is blamed for a task she did not perform.
She has relevant information showing that someone else was responsible.
Expected lesson: Employees can challenge inaccurate corrections without hostility.
list: Should the employee accept blame simply to avoid conflict?
How can she explain the facts respectfully?
What should the supervisor do before reaching a conclusion?
When might further review or escalation be appropriate?

sections.title: 16. Practical group activity: Respond without hostility
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees practise responding calmly and respectfully when receiving correction.
Divide participants into pairs. One person gives a workplace correction, and the other practises responding professionally.
Expected outcome: Participants should learn to receive correction without aggression, unnecessary arguments or retaliation.
table: "I understand. Please explain what needs to be corrected."
"Could we clarify who was responsible for the task?"
"My understanding is different. May I explain?"
"I understand the concern. What should I improve?"
"I'll review my responsibility and address the issue."

sections.title: Role-play exercise
list: The supervisor identifies a missed room-preparation step.
The employee listens without interrupting.
The employee applies the CALM method.
The employee asks a clarifying question.
Both agree on the next appropriate action.

sections.title: 17. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 4 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What does receiving correction without hostility mean? Agreeing with every accusation / Listening, evaluating the concern and responding respectfully / Remaining silent even when the correction is unfair
A supervisor corrects your work. What is the best response? Listen and ask for clarification where necessary / Raise your voice immediately / Walk away angrily
Which behaviour is an example of hostility? Asking for a private discussion / Explaining relevant facts calmly / Insulting or threatening the person giving correction
What does the CALM method encourage? Avoiding all corrections / Controlling reactions, assessing feedback, learning and making adjustments / Blaming others for mistakes

What should an employee do when a correction is inaccurate? Explain the facts respectfully and request clarification or review / Accept false blame without question / Retaliate against the person giving correction

sections.title: 18. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what receiving correction without hostility means.
Identify five examples of hostile reactions to correction.
Explain the difference between humility and humiliation.
Describe three reasons employees may react angrily when corrected.
Explain the CALM method in your own words.
Describe how you would respond if a supervisor corrected you for a genuine mistake.
Explain how you would respond if you were wrongly blamed for an incomplete task.
Describe how employees should respond when colleagues identify genuine work-related mistakes.
Explain why retaliation after receiving correction is harmful to teamwork.
Identify three habits you intend to develop to receive corrections more professionally.

sections.title: 19. Seven-day correction challenge
table: Avoid raising your voice when corrected
Ask a clarifying question before reacting
Acknowledge a genuine mistake without unnecessary excuses
Apply the CALM method during a difficult conversation
Reflect on how your response to correction has improved

sections.title: 20. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Correction is a normal part of professional development.
Every employee will sometimes need guidance, clarification or improvement.
At Zura Spa, employees should learn to receive correction without unnecessary anger, insults, threats or retaliation.
They should listen carefully, examine the facts, acknowledge genuine mistakes and take appropriate corrective action.
Supervisors and colleagues must also communicate corrections respectfully, fairly and constructively.
Next topic: Admitting Mistakes and Apologising Sincerely.

remember: Correction is not automatically rejection, and feedback is not automatically an attack. A professional employee is willing to listen, learn and improve without allowing pride or anger to control the conversation. At Zura Spa, humility means recognising that improvement is always possible. Receive valid correction with maturity, explain your perspective with respect and allow every genuine learning opportunity to make you better.
